newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian govt sees meat sector reform soon.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian govt sees meat sector reform soon.

text.p: The Australian government would move at an early stage to ensure that differences in proposed details of reform in the meat sector were reconciled as far as possible, Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said.
Anderson was commenting after the government's release of a major report on meat and livestock industry reform.
The government would move to ensure that the most suitable changes were implemented, Anderson said in a statement.
Speaking in parliament after the release of the report, Anderson said a final decision on meat sector reform would be made in January.

"All of this will constitute a vitally important link in the ground up restoration of Australia's rural industries, reflecting our rebuilding of the economic and social infrastructure of regional Australia," he said.

The report presented as a preferred option the replacement of the main industry statutory body the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) with two separate entities, one for beef the other for sheepmeat.

It recommended that the industry's three existing statutory bodies, the Meat Research Corp (MRC), the AMLC and the Meat Industry Council (MIC) be abolished and replaced with two non-statutory authorities.

The report also contained minority recommendations, one calling for the establishment of a single meat corporation with separate operational units and the other for the establishment of one corporation with two product-focussed business units.
"It is clear the stakeholders (in the meat industry) are seeking significant reform, although there remains some important differences in the details," Anderson said.

"I will now work actively with relevant industry and government reeperesentatives to address the need for new levy-based institutional structures to administer collective marketing and research and development services," he said.
The AMLC said in a statement that it welcomed the report, undertaken by consultants Coopers and Lybrand.

AMLC chairman John Kerin said that while the report was favourable on both the effectiveness of AMLC programs and the efficiency of corporate operations, it highlighted some areas where improvements could be made.

The report had said the AMLC had been successful in maintaining an awareness of Australian lamb and beef as desirable food products in Australia and raising awareness and promoting market growth in overseas markets, Kerin said.

The report also said the AMLC had been operating in a very difficult business and that without the AMLC it was likely that Australia's performance in overseas markets would have been significantly worse, Kerin said.
Changes recommended would see further simplification of the management structure and consideration of more "outsourcing" of current services, he said. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
